title: Radiators and Glasshouse
premise: Paloma Sandoval, a bridge inspector who measures everything—including her marriage—in millimeters of wear, discovers a box of undelivered letters behind her late grandmother's wardrobe, written by a woman the family erased. As she and her husband Teo restore the family glasshouse slated for demolition, the letters force each relative to confront the arranged silence that shaped them all. Paloma must choose between preserving the family's careful architecture of duty or letting it crack open into something honest. The novel ends on demolition day: the glasshouse stands, rebuilt by reluctant hands, while Paloma finally says aloud what she has only measured in silence.
about_author: Emrys Vasquez is the pen name of a former structural engineer who spent a decade inspecting bridges across the American Southwest before turning to fiction. Their work explores how families, like structures, fail slowly and then suddenly.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. On-site at a decaying overpass, Paloma catalogs cracks with forensic calm, then returns home to a dinner where she and Teo exchange pleasantries like load reports. Emotional beat: competent numbness; she trusts steel more than speech.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Clearing her grandmother Mercedes's house for sale, Paloma finds a box of forty years of unsent letters behind the wardrobe—addressed to someone named Aurelio. Emotional beat: curiosity sharpening into unease as the first letter reveals an engagement no one mentioned.

chapters.title: Load-Bearing Walls
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo notices Paloma pulling away and responds by fixing things—the gutters, the car, anything but conversation. He remembers his own mother's silence. Emotional beat: love expressed as maintenance, misread as indifference.

chapters.title: Aurelio
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She tracks down records: Aurelio Reyes, a gardener who worked the family glasshouse until 1974, dismissed without explanation. Her aunt Rosa warns her to leave it. Emotional beat: first crack in the family's official story.

chapters.title: The Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma visits the derelict glasshouse on the family's last parcel of land, scheduled for demolition. Among broken panes she finds initials scratched in a frame. Emotional beat: grief for a place she never knew mattered.

chapters.title: What Rosa Kept
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Rosa admits she knew about Mercedes and Aurelio—and that she helped end it, believing she was protecting her sister from scandal. Emotional beat: guilt worn so long it feels like virtue.

chapters.title: Hairline Fractures
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. A fight about selling the house exposes deeper fault lines: Teo wants children; Paloma has never said no, only nothing. Emotional beat: the marriage's deferred question surfaces, echoing the letters' central one.

chapters.title: Letters, Unsent
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Reading deeper into the box, Paloma finds Mercedes kept writing after Aurelio left—decades of letters describing the family from behind glass. Emotional beat: recognition; Paloma sees her own watchful silence inherited whole.

chapters.title: Cousins
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At a family lunch, Paloma tests the waters; cousin Dani admits she always sensed something unspoken 'arranged around the table like furniture.' Emotional beat: solidarity forming against the older generation's code.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The county confirms the glasshouse comes down in eleven weeks. Paloma petitions to delay, using her professional standing. Emotional beat: first time Paloma spends her credibility on something personal.

chapters.title: Teo's Inheritance
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo visits his own estranged father, seeking a model for repair, and finds only another man who maintained things instead of mending them. Emotional beat: understanding that silence is also inherited property.

chapters.title: Rosa Breaks
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Confronted with the final letter—Mercedes asking forgiveness—Rosa confesses she intercepted Aurelio's replies and returned them unopened. Emotional beat: shame collapsing into relief; the secret loses its weight by being spoken.

chapters.title: Where He Went
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Following a return address, Paloma learns Aurelio lived ninety miles away, ran a nursery, died two years prior—with a daughter, Lucía, who has the letters he wrote back. Emotional beat: hope complicated by lateness.

chapters.title: Lucía
chapters.summary: Lucía's POV. Lucía, wary, shows Paloma her father's side: forty years of answered letters he never sent, waiting for permission. Emotional beat: two inheritances of cowardice meeting across a kitchen table.

chapters.title: Stress Test
chapters.summary: Paloma and Teo's alternating POV. Paloma asks Teo the deferred question directly—does he want to stay?—and they argue honestly for the first time in years. Emotional beat: painful aliveness replacing polite deadness.

chapters.title: The Family Arranges Itself
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. An emergency family meeting over the letters fractures the relatives into defenders of silence and seekers of truth. Emotional beat: the architecture of duty visibly failing under load.

chapters.title: Mercedes, Whole
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The last letter, written in Mercedes's final year, asks not forgiveness but witness: 'Let someone know I was here.' Emotional beat: Paloma understands the demolition isn't of glass—it's of erasure.

chapters.title: Joint Inspection
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo, unasked, files to co-sponsor the glasshouse preservation as a heritage structure, spending his own standing beside hers. Emotional beat: love shown as structural support rather than maintenance.

chapters.title: Reckoning
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The family gathers at the glasshouse; Rosa reads Mercedes's final letter aloud to everyone, including Lucía. Old accusations flare, then exhaust themselves. Emotional beat: catharsis through shared witness.

chapters.title: Panels
chapters.summary: Paloma, Teo, Dani, and Lucía's POV. The cousins and spouses begin restoring the glasshouse themselves, pane by pane, the week before demolition. Emotional beat: belonging built by hand rather than granted by blood.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The county arrives; the preserved structure stands, reclassified. Paloma speaks at the small ceremony—naming Mercedes and Aurelio publicly, saying aloud what the family arranged itself around. Emotional beat: voice replacing measurement.

chapters.title: Radiators
chapters.summary: Paloma and Teo's alternating POV. Winter: the restored glasshouse glows warm, radiators ticking. Paloma and Teo, still imperfect, plant something together and answer each other plainly. Emotional beat: quiet, earned resolution—love as ongoing inspection, willingly performed.
